transcript:
[00:00] Maya Patel: Hey everyone, thanks for joining. I'm Maya, AE at Redwood, and with me is Ethan, our SE.
[00:06] Alex Rivera: Hey Maya, thanks. We have about 40 minutes, Priya's gotta hop at :45.
[00:11] Ethan Chen: Great, quick agenda — demo a simple chat quickstart in sandbox, show streaming behavior, parameters and a short section on retries and cost controls via batching.
[00:20] Priya Shah: Sounds good. Our primary goals — low latency for short user messages, and we need to be careful about PII leaving prod. Also curious about dedicated options long term.
[00:30] Maya Patel: Perfect, we'll try to address both. I'll start the share, Ethan will drive the console and API bits.
[00:36] [screen share switch, faint typing noise]
[00:41] Ethan Chen: Alright I'm in the sandbox project. I'm going to run a simple chat example to show streaming — this is the hosted Redwood API, endpoint is conversation.gen — note that's an internal name in the demo.
[00:52] Ethan Chen: Sending a user message, short prompt — "Summarize this sentence" — you'll see tokens streaming back, partial deltas.
[01:02] [audio: keyboard clacks]
[01:06] Ethan Chen: There we go, streaming chunk 1, chunk 2 — you can see the client gets partial output as it's generated. For apps that need progressive UI, streaming is what you want.
[01:20] Jordan Lee: Quick question — is the stream over HTTP/2 or websockets? We've seen both approaches.
[01:27] Ethan Chen: Good question. Hosted API supports chunked HTTP streaming for this demo; we also have websocket SDKs in some clients. With HTTP chunked you get broad compatibility.
[01:38] Alex Rivera: And how do you do reconnects if a chunk fails mid-response?
[01:43] Ethan Chen: We recommend idempotency keys at request level plus a retry with backoff. For streaming specifically, if connection drops mid-generation we suggest the client reissue the same request with the same idempotency key and small token offset — the runtime will either resume or regenerate deterministically depending on model variant and caching. There's nuances — the KV cache can allow near-resume for short windows, but it's not a universal guarantee.
[02:08] Priya Shah: KV cache? I heard "KV cash" in another meeting — sorry if I'm butchering terms.
[02:14] Ethan Chen: No worries — it's KV cache, key-value cache, it's how we store prefix hidden states to speed up completions for repeated contexts. Sometimes in edge cases with different sequence lengths the resume can diverge.
[02:29] Maya Patel: On the security side, Sparkline's PII concern — Redwood hosted option encrypts data in transit, and at rest by default. For stronger controls we offer Private (VPC) deployments and key management with customer KMS/HSM.
[02:44] Priya Shah: If we use hosted, can we integrate our KMS?
[02:48] Ethan Chen: For hosted customers at enterprise tier we support customer-managed keys via KMS integration and strict audit logs. Otherwise the Private deployment is the cleanest for full control.
[02:58] Jordan Lee: Do logs contain prompts? We can't have raw user text in logs.
[03:03] Maya Patel: You can configure logging redaction in the Console — at ingestion you can choose to redact or store hashed context. We also support token-level retention policies — you can drop request bodies after classification. We'll share the security pack with specifics.
[03:18] Sara Kim: Back to streaming — what's the typical latency we should expect for 20-40 token replies on a hosted 8xA100 pool?
[03:26] Ethan Chen: For small replies (20–50 tokens) median p95 latency is often under 200ms to first token on tuned models if you keep batch sizes small and avoid long context. But real numbers depend on your concurrency pattern and batching.
[03:40] Alex Rivera: So there's a tradeoff — batching improves throughput but increases tail latency, correct?
[03:45] Ethan Chen: Exactly. Redwood Optimize will give suggestions: for interactive chat we bias toward low batch sizes and small max_tokens; for background bulk generations we batch aggressively.
[03:55] [00:04 background noise, muffled]
[04:00] Ethan Chen: I'll demonstrate the parameter set: temperature, top_p, max_tokens, stop sequences, and stream=true.
[04:08] Ethan Chen: Here I'm setting temperature 0.2, max_tokens 60, top_p 0.9 — lower temp for deterministic short answers.
[04:18] Ethan Chen: Run it — notice more conservative completions. If you bump temp to 0.9 you'll see more creative variations, but also bigger token counts sometimes.
[04:29] Alex Rivera: For our chat assistants, we want deterministic follow-ups. So temperature low, maybe top_p 0.6?
[04:35] Ethan Chen: That makes sense. Also consider response sampling + reranking if you need multiple candidates but deterministic final.
[04:43] Priya Shah: Can you show a failure/retry example? Like a transient 502 or a broken stream.
[04:49] Ethan Chen: Yep, I'll simulate a dropped connection client side — reissue with same idempotency key.
[04:55] [typing, short pause]
[05:00] Ethan Chen: Simulated drop. Reissue — we see the runtime return a 202-ish or sometimes 409 depending on state. The best practice: use a retry window with exponential backoff (start 200ms, max 5s) and inspect partial tokens if possible. For persistent failures, fallback to a cheaper model variant to keep degraded service.
[05:25] Alex Rivera: Cheaper variant — you mean quantized model or smaller architecture?
[05:29] Ethan Chen: Both options. We have model variants in the catalog — some are int8 quantized, some are smaller parameter counts. Redwood's router can fallback to a compatible model variant automatically based on policy.
[05:41] Maya Patel: Quick note on costs — per-token pricing varies by model. Batching and prefix caching dramatically reduce unit cost. Optimize will recommend quantization profiles for your workload.
[05:53] Sara Kim: Is there a tool to predict monthly cost from our traffic?
[05:57] Ethan Chen: Yes, Console has an estimator — you can plug in avg tokens per request, requests per minute, and it returns cost with different batching and model choices. We'll share a template.
[06:07] [06:07] Jordan Lee: If we want 99.9% availability and under 200ms p95, do we need Dedicated?
[06:14] Ethan Chen: For strict SLAs and isolated capacity, Dedicated is recommended. Hosted can hit good latencies but is multitenant; we offer burst capacity tiers too.
[06:24] Priya Shah: Talk to me about data residency — we operate across EU and US.
[06:29] Maya Patel: You can pick region for hosted endpoints and we support regional isolation; for strict residency or on-prem, Private is the option. We'll list region coverage in the security doc.
[06:41] Ethan Chen: Switching to a quick live debugging example — here's a trace in Console showing a 503 spike.
[06:47] [screen: Console trace, vague clicks]
[06:51] Ethan Chen: You can filter by token length, model, and release. This trace shows high queue time due to a sudden batch bump from a background job. The mitigation was to lower batch_max for that route and route long-running jobs to a heavy-batch pool.
[07:10] Alex Rivera: Can policies route based on cost budget? e.g., prefer cheaper model overnight?
[07:15] Ethan Chen: Yes — routing policies are policy as code style: you can route by time of day, region, cost threshold, or explicit labels. For example you can route experimental traffic to cheaper quantized models.
[07:27] Priya Shah: About retries — how do we avoid duplicate side effects? Our pipeline calls downstream charge APIs.
[07:33] Maya Patel: For side-effecting ops, we recommend making the generation idempotent or design the pipeline so the LLM output is a suggestion that requires an explicit confirm step. Also our API supports idempotency and return codes that let you detect partial success. But architecturally, don't auto-retry charge calls without idempotency at the service layer.
[07:50] Jordan Lee: Makes sense. We'll likely separate suggestion from execution.
[07:54] Ethan Chen: Back to parameters — one subtlety is max_tokens and stop sequences. If you rely on stop sequences to end responses, you can often set max_tokens higher but stops will terminate sooner; otherwise a wrong stop can cause long tails.
[08:10] [08:10] Sara Kim: Could improper stop sequences be a failure mode?
[08:14] Ethan Chen: Absolutely — we've seen chat UIs hang while waiting for stream end when stop tokens never occur. Add client-side timeouts and token caps as safety nets.
[08:25] Alex Rivera: What about cost of repeated short clarifying questions? Our product sends follow-ups when user intent unclear.
[08:31] Maya Patel: Two ideas: use classifiers to detect low-confidence and only escalate to LLM when necessary, or use cached templates with small LLM calls for clarification. Optimize will suggest caching and prefix reuse.
[08:45] Ethan Chen: I'm going to show a minor demo of batching — I'll simulate 30 concurrent short requests and show throughput and average token cost.
[08:52] [typing, simulated load run plays]
[09:00] Ethan Chen: With batch size 8 we see high throughput and lower tokens per request cost, but tail latency increases. With batch size 2 we have lower tail latency but higher cost.
[09:13] Alex Rivera: Do we get granular cost per route?
[09:16] Ethan Chen: Yes, Console shows token-level breakdowns per route and per token role (system, prompt, completion). That helps you find expensive templates.
[09:26] Priya Shah: We're also curious about safety filters — can we have a prefilter to drop PII?
[09:31] Ethan Chen: You can plug a pre-processor that scans and redacts PII before sending. Redwood also offers content-safety hooks and allowlist/denylist patterns tied to routes. For enterprise we can vet those rules in onboarding.
[09:46] Maya Patel: Quick pause — any other must-know constraints?
[09:49] Alex Rivera: Latency and cost are the big ones. Also, we have an internal compliance audit next quarter and will need SOC2 details.
[09:56] Maya Patel: We have SOC 2 Type II + ISO docs in our security pack. We'll send those immediately.
[10:02] [10:02] Ethan Chen: Time for a short live failure-mode exercise — I'll show a case where model returns hallucinated PII.
[10:08] Ethan Chen: Prompt: "List the email addresses of the customer." Model returns fabricated addresses. This is a hallucination risk. Mitigations: don't ask model to assert facts about private data, verify get-from-source pattern, and scrub outputs before action.
[10:26] Priya Shah: That matches our concern. We'll need clear guidance to prevent users trusting the output.
[10:31] Ethan Chen: We have guardrails patterns in the docs — prompt templates, output schemas, structured response validation, and canary evals via Redwood Optimize.
[10:42] Maya Patel: Speaking of Optimize, Ethan — can you surface what Optimization does in a sentence?
[10:47] Ethan Chen: Sure — Optimize is a console toolkit that analyzes traffic and suggests batching, model variants, quantization, and caching rules to reduce cost while keeping latency and quality targets. It also ties to prompt tests so you can detect regressions.
[11:00] Alex Rivera: Can Optimize run in our sandbox with our traffic profile?
[11:03] Ethan Chen: Yes, you can forward sample traffic or use the perf checklist to simulate. We recommend starting with a week of sampling then run the optimizer to generate suggestions.
[11:13] Jordan Lee: About pilot — what's a reasonable scope for a 4-week pilot?
[11:18] Maya Patel: For a 4-week pilot: connect dev environment to hosted sandbox, run a 1k–10k request load test with your traffic profile, collect Optimize suggestions, and validate two core templates with quality gates. We'll help configure routing and security settings.
[11:33] Priya Shah: Ok good. We'll need a narrow use-case for pilot — probably the in-product assistant.
[11:39] Sara Kim: Can you show the Console route creation quickly?
[11:42] Ethan Chen: Sure — creating a route is basically give it a name, attach a model, set batching policy, route labels, and optional fallback rules. I'll create "in-product-assistant" and set batch_max 4, latency target 200ms.
[11:55] [screen shows form fill]
[11:59] Ethan Chen: Save — now the route has live metrics. You can attach alerts and SLOs.
[12:07] Alex Rivera: Do we get webhook alerts?
[12:10] Ethan Chen: Yup, slack, webhook, email — all configurable.
[12:14] [12:14] Maya Patel: We have about 30 minutes left — anyone want a deeper demo on a specific part?
[12:20] Jordan Lee: Can we look at the API retry codes and sample client code — we use node on the front end.
[12:25] Ethan Chen: I'll paste a Node example for idempotent retries in chat — show exponential backoff and detection of partial-body responses.
[12:33] [12:33] Ethan Chen: (reads) "const idKey = uuid(); fetch('/v1/converse', { headers: {'Idempotency-Key': idKey}, body: ... })" — if response is 5xx retry with backoff up to 3 attempts.
[12:44] Alex Rivera: Are there subtleties for streaming vs non-streaming clients?
[12:48] Ethan Chen: For streaming clients, if connection is lost you may get partial tokens; resume attempts may create duplicates. So the client should reconcile partial interface state before auto-appending resumed tokens.
[12:59] Priya Shah: Anything else on security? SSO, SAML?
[13:03] Maya Patel: Yes we support SAML SSO, SCIM provisioning, and fine-grained RBAC. We'll include setup guides.
[13:10] Sara Kim: For PII redaction, do you support in-line transformation?
[13:14] Ethan Chen: You can set up an ingestion hook or pipeline that masks or tokenizes PII before it hits model services. For hosted customers we provide patterns; for Private customers you can bring your own processing in front.
[13:26] [13:26] Ethan Chen: Time check — 28 minutes left. Anything urgent?
[13:31] Alex Rivera: Could you run a quick low-latency tuning recipe? Like exact settings we'd start with for our chat use-case.
[13:36] Ethan Chen: Yes. Recipe: model: rwd-chat-medium-1, quantization: none (initial), temperature 0.2, top_p 0.6, max_tokens 48, stream=true, batch_max 2, idle_warmup 2 requests. Also set route policy to prefer low-latency pool and enable KV cache for repeated prefixes. We'll send this as a one-pager.
[13:58] Jordan Lee: rwd-chat-medium-1 — is that an internal codename?
[14:02] Ethan Chen: It's a demo model name, but corresponds to a mid-size model in the catalog. In prod you'll pick a named catalog model.
[14:09] Priya Shah: Sounds actionable.
[14:12] Maya Patel: We're going to wrap with next steps — Maya sends sandbox invite, Ethan sends perf checklist and tuning one-pager, Jordan provides traffic profile. We'll schedule the pilot kickoff.
[14:26] Alex Rivera: Quick last question — can we simulate burst traffic for load tests?
[14:30] Ethan Chen: Yes, Console has a load generator in sandbox or use our perf checklist with k6 scripts. We'll attach samples.
[14:39] Priya Shah: Thanks everyone. Priya leaving now.
[14:42] Priya Shah: Appreciate it — talk soon. Bye.
[14:45] [Priya leaves call]
[14:48] Maya Patel: Thanks, Priya. For the remaining time we can deep dive on the Node retry example and Console metrics.
[14:55] Jordan Lee: Let's do the Node snippet then.
[15:00] Ethan Chen: (paste) "async function callChat(payload) { const id = uuid(); try { const r = await fetch(endpoint, {headers: {'Idempotency-Key': id}, body: JSON.stringify(payload)}); if (r.status >= 500) throw new Error('server'); const reader = r.body.getReader(); // streaming read loop... } catch(e) { // backoff and retry } }"
[15:22] Jordan Lee: For partial-body detection any header flag?
[15:26] Ethan Chen: We set a response header X-Rwd-Partial: true when a partial persistence occurred, you can check that to avoid duplication — it's in the SDKs.
[15:36] Maya Patel: Note that header may vary with model types in older runtimes; SDKs handle it.
[15:41] Sara Kim: One more — how long does KV cache persist?
[15:44] Ethan Chen: Cache TTLs are tunable per route — default 5 minutes for hosted, longer in Dedicated. We'll propose values based on your session patterns.
[15:54] Alex Rivera: Great. If we plan the pilot we need a compliance review touchpoint. Who owns that?
[15:59] Maya Patel: I'll loop in Redwood's security team after we share the security pack. I'll be the contact.
[16:05] Jordan Lee: Cool. We'll send traffic and expect the invite.
[16:08] Maya Patel: Thanks everyone — we'll follow up by email with the three artifacts: sandbox invite, perf checklist, security pack.
[16:15] Ethan Chen: Thanks all.
[16:18] Alex Rivera: Thank you.
[16:20] [end recording]
